title: Orcas Play Food-Smashing Game with Giant Sunfish!
summary: Have you ever seen a video of orcas hunting? They're super smart and work as a team. But scientists just saw something totally new. In the Gulf of California, orcas were filmed smashing a giant sunfish into thousands of tiny pieces! A sunfish can be longer than a car and weigh as much as a small truck—up to 2,000 kg. That's like 30 grown-ups! One orca held the dead sunfish by its tail. Then another orca swam really fast and rammed into it. At the last second, the first orca let go. The hit was so strong that the fish broke apart into a cloud of bits. A young orca then ate the small pieces, while the adults ate the rest. Scientists think this might be a way for orca parents to help their babies eat more easily. Or maybe they were just playing—orcas are known for playing with their food! This happened twice, once in 2024 and again in 2025. The sunfish were already dead, so the orcas weren't killing them. They were breaking the food into smaller bites. The fish has a jelly-like outer layer, and when it breaks, tiny living things inside spread into the water. This might change the water's nutrients. Scientists are excited because no one has ever seen orcas use ramming to process food before. They want more videos to learn if the same orcas did it both times. Next time you see orcas, remember—they might be playing a wild game of food-smash!
why_it_matters: Like orca parents, the people who care for you also break big challenges into small, easy steps so you can learn and grow.

background_read: Orcas, also called killer whales, are actually the largest members of the dolphin family. They live in family groups called pods and are known for their clever hunting tricks.
The Gulf of California is a sea surrounded by Mexico. It’s home to many amazing animals, including the giant ocean sunfish—the heaviest bony fish in the world.
Article_Structure: WHO: A group of orcas (including adults and a youngster) in the Gulf of California.
WHAT: Filmed using a new ramming technique to shatter a dead giant sunfish into tiny, edible pieces.
WHERE: In the warm waters of the Gulf of California, off the coast of Mexico.
WHY: Scientists think it might be a way to help young orcas eat more easily, or just a playful food-smashing game.

perspectives.description: Orca mothers may be teaching their calves how to eat and survive by making food easier to handle, showing how smart and social these animals are.
Orcas are famous for playing with their prey, so it might just be a rowdy game—not a serious feeding lesson. That makes them seem more like teenagers having fun.
